claims.text: Replacing approximately 2 at.% Cr with Hf in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress Cr-V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
The approximately 2 at.% Hf substitution will preserve the alloy's low irradiation hardening and radiation resistance.
The approximately 2 at.% Hf substitution will preserve practical bulk manufacturability.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr-V-rich precipitates under energetic-particle irradiation at about 8 dpa.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 otherwise has good radiation resistance and low irradiation hardening.
The Cr-V-rich precipitates potentially degrade the irradiated baseline alloy.
A specimen-temperature range of 1250–1600 K reflects fusion-relevant operating temperatures.
Hf will promote stable, finely dispersed Hf-based nanoscale clusters or modify grain-boundary chemistry.
The Hf-induced clusters or grain-boundary chemistry changes will disrupt nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich phases.
Hf addition will alter local thermodynamic and kinetic conditions and reduce the driving force for irradiation-induced Cr-V precipitation.
The Hf modification could enhance irradiation-defect annihilation at interfaces and grain boundaries.
Enhanced defect annihilation and matrix stability will maintain low hardening and good radiation resistance.
At up to 8 dpa and 1250–1600 K, the Hf-modified alloy will have significantly fewer or smaller Cr-V-rich precipitates than the baseline.
At up to 8 dpa and 1250–1600 K, the Hf-modified alloy will have hardening and radiation resistance comparable to the baseline.
The Hf-modified alloy will introduce no additional complications in bulk processing.
The proposed mitigation may not persist beyond 8 dpa or outside 1250–1600 K.
The optimal Hf concentration and the long-term thermal stability of the modified alloy remain undetermined.
Minor Hf substitution may produce additional secondary phases.
